claim: FGF produced in the larval wing imaginal-disc moves to the air-sac-primordium (ASP) through FGFR-containing cytonemes that extend from the ASP to contact the wing-disc source.
source: FGF produced in the larval wing imaginal-disc moves to the air-sac-primordium (ASP) through FGFR-containing cytonemes that extend from the ASP to contact the wing-disc source.
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing Bnl:GFP distribution from wing disc to ASP (Figures 1C-D', 3C-J), FGFR (Btl:Cherry) localization on cytonemes (Figures 2, 3H), and cytoneme contacts with the source (Figures 3I-J, 5D-D'', Video 3).

claim: The number of FGF-receiving cytonemes extended by ASP cells decreases gradually with increasing distance from the source, generating a recipient-specific FGF gradient.
source: The number of FGF-receiving cytonemes extended by ASP cells decreases gradually with increasing distance from the source, generating a recipient-specific FGF gradient.
evidence: Figure 5A-D'' shows quantitative analysis of cytoneme numbers and orientations from different ASP regions, demonstrating a gradient in cytoneme numbers correlating with distance from the source.

claim: FGF activates concentration-dependent gene expression in the ASP, inducing pointed-P1 at higher and cut at lower levels.
source: Acting as a morphogen in the ASP, FGF activates concentration-dependent gene expression, inducing pointed-P1 at higher and cut at lower levels.
evidence: Figure 6A-E shows spatial expression domains of sty, pntP1, cut, and yan correlating with Bnl:GFP gradient levels. Figure 6H-L demonstrates that Bnl overexpression expands pntP1 domain and suppresses cut domain.

claim: The transcription-factors Pointed-P1 and Cut antagonize each other and differentially regulate formation of FGFR-containing cytonemes.
source: The transcription-factors Pointed-P1 and Cut antagonize each other and differentially regulate formation of FGFR-containing cytonemes, creating regions with higher-to-lower numbers of FGF-receiving cytonemes.
evidence: Figure 6M-P shows reciprocal inhibition between PntP1 and Cut. Figure 7 demonstrates that Cut GOF suppresses cytonemes (7A-B'), while PntP1 GOF induces cytonemes (7C,C') and PntP1 LOF suppresses cytonemes (7D-E').

claim: Bnl:GFP expressed at physiological levels from the bnl:gfpendo allele moved from the disc bnl-source to the ASP and distributed along the distal to proximal direction of the recipient tissue.
source: Bnl:GFP, produced at physiological level from the bnl:gfpendo allele, moved from the disc bnl-source to the ASP and distributed along the distal to proximal direction of the recipient tissue; (C,C') bnl-source marked by CherryCAAX expression (bnl-LexA, lexO-CherryCAAX/bnl:gfpendo); (D,D') recipient ASP marked by CD8:Cherry expression (btl-Gal4,UAS-CD8:Cherry/+; bnl:gfpendo)
evidence: Figure 1C-D' shows fluorescence imaging of Bnl:GFP distribution from source to ASP. The bnl:gfpendo allele was generated by CRISPR/Cas9 genome editing (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).

claim: Bnl:GFP forms a long-range exponential gradient spanning ~100–120 μm in range in late third instar larval ASPs.
source: Measurement of Bnl:GFP intensities along the longest D-P axis of the late third instar larval ASPs revealed a long-range exponential gradient spanning ~100–120 μm in range.
evidence: Figure 1E shows quantitative measurement of Bnl:GFP gradient with exponential fit (N = 4 independent samples).

claim: The signal concentration decreased exponentially toward the proximal ASP stalk as the distance from the source increased.
source: The signal concentration decreased exponentially toward the proximal ASP stalk as the distance from the source increased.
evidence: Figure 1E shows exponential decay of Bnl:GFP intensity along the D-P axis.

claim: The Bnl:GFP gradient shapes developed concomitantly with the growth of the recipient ASP.
source: The Bnl:GFP gradient shapes were variable, and developed concomitantly with the growth of the recipient ASP (Figure 1F).
evidence: Figure 1F shows time-course imaging of Bnl:GFP distribution at different developmental stages (18-26h, 32-40h, 45-50h, 55-60h after third instar larval molt).

claim: In shorter early third instar larval ASPs, Bnl:GFP formed relatively steeper and narrower gradients (slope ~3.14) compared to larger/longer late-stage ASPs (slope ~0.71).
source: In the shorter early third instar larval ASPs (~35–40 hr after third instar larval molt), Bnl:GFP formed relatively steeper and narrower gradients (slope of a straight line joining Cmax to C1/2max =~3.14) compared to the larger/longer late-stage ASPs (slope =~0.71) (Figure 1E,G).
evidence: Figure 1G shows gradient measurements in early third instar larvae (N = 3 independent samples) with steeper slope compared to Figure 1E (late third instar).

claim: A strong negative correlation of the gradient slopes with the length of the ASP D-P axis was observed in a population of randomly harvested wandering third instar larval ASPs.
source: A strong negative correlation of the gradient slopes with the length of the ASP D-P axis was also observed in a population of randomly harvested wandering third instar larval ASPs, which showed natural developmental variations in size (Figure 1H).
evidence: Figure 1H shows scatter plot with R² = 0.94585 demonstrating negative correlation between ASP D-P axis length and gradient slope.

claim: Animals that harbored the bnl:gfpendo knock-in allele were homozygous viable, had normal tissue morphology, and the expected gene expression patterns.
source: Animals that harbored the bnl:gfpendo knock-in allele were homozygous viable, had normal tissue morphology, and the expected gene expression patterns (Du et al., 2017; Sato and Kornberg, 2002).
evidence: Figure 1—figure supplement 1C shows efficiency table indicating normal morphology and gene expression were verified. The statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: All of the detectable bright fluorescent Bnl:GFP puncta outside of the source cells were asymmetrically distributed only in the recipient ASP cells.
source: As a paracrine signal, Bnl was expected to disperse and form a continuous gradient surrounding the wing disc source (Figure 1A'). However, all of the detectable bright fluorescent Bnl:GFP puncta outside of the source cells were asymmetrically distributed only in the recipient ASP cells (Figure 1C–D').
evidence: Figure 1C-D' shows fluorescence imaging demonstrating Bnl:GFP puncta localized specifically in ASP, not in surrounding wing disc cells or myoblasts (Videos 1 and 2).

claim: Although Bnl:GFP moved from the wing disc source to the ASP, the punctate signal did not localize in the non-specific wing disc cells surrounding the signal source or in the myoblast cells located between the disc source and the ASP.
source: Thus, although Bnl:GFP moved from the wing disc source to the ASP, the punctate signal did not localize in the non-specific wing disc cells surrounding the signal source or in the myoblast cells located between the disc source and the ASP (Videos 1 and 2).
evidence: Videos 1 and 2 show serial Z-stacks demonstrating asymmetric Bnl:GFP localization only in ASP, not in surrounding tissues.

claim: The Bnl antibody recognized all of the Bnl:GFP puncta in the larval ASP, confirming that they represent the Bnl protein.
source: The Bnl antibody recognized all of the Bnl:GFP puncta in the larval ASP, confirming that they represent the Bnl protein (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,A').
evidence: Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,A' shows immunostaining with αBnl antibody (red) recognizing Bnl:GFP puncta in the ASP.

claim: Overexpression of bnlRNAi from the disc bnl-source in the bnl:gfpendo larvae knocked down both Bnl:GFP expression and ASP growth in most samples.
source: As expected, overexpression of bnlRNAi from the disc bnl-source in the bnl:gfpendo larvae knocked down both Bnl:GFP expression and ASP growth in most samples, indicating that the tagged signaling protein is functional (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B–C).
evidence: Figure 1—figure supplement 2B-C shows phenotypic analysis of bnlRNAi-mediated knockdown with table showing 43/50 samples had loss of Bnl:GFP and lack of ASP.

claim: Samples with low levels of Bnl:GFP after incomplete RNAi-mediated knock-down had small, stunted ASPs with a shallow range of Bnl:GFP distribution.
source: However, due to incomplete RNAi-mediated knock-down of bnl:gfpendo, a few samples still contained low levels of Bnl:GFP. Importantly, these samples also had small, stunted ASPs with a shallow range of Bnl:GFP distribution. This correlation between Bnl:GFP levels/distribution and ASP growth suggested that the levels and distribution of Bnl:GFP in the ASP have a significant developmental role (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B–C).
evidence: Figure 1—figure supplement 2B'' shows example of partial knockdown with reduced ASP growth. The table in 2C shows 7/50 samples with incomplete suppression and partial ASP growth.

claim: Btl:Cherry expressed at physiological levels marked all tracheal cells and formed a concentration gradient along the D-P axis of the ASP.
source: As expected, Btl:Cherry expressed at physiological levels marked all tracheal cells, but formed a concentration gradient along the D-P axis of the ASP (Figure 2B; Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D show fluorescence imaging and intensity plots of Btl:Cherry gradient in ASP.

claim: This observation is consistent with an earlier report describing activation of btl transcription by Bnl signaling.
source: This observation is consistent with an earlier report describing activation of btl transcription by Bnl signaling (Ohshiro et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim references a previous publication (Ohshiro et al., 2002) that reported btl transcriptional activation by Bnl signaling.

claim: In trans-heterozygous btl:cherryendo/bnl:gfpendo animals, all the Bnl:GFP puncta in the ASP colocalized with Btl:Cherry and the receptor gradient coincided with that of the ligand gradient.
source: In trans-heterozygous btl:cherryendo/bnl:gfpendo animals, all the Bnl:GFP puncta in the ASP colocalized with Btl:Cherry and the receptor gradient coincided with that of the ligand gradient (Figure 2C–D; Figure 2—figure supplement 1E,E').
evidence: Figure 2C-D shows colocalization of Bnl:GFP and Btl:Cherry with overlapping intensity gradients. Figure 2—figure supplement 1E,E' shows additional examples.

claim: A small number of receptor-ligand puncta were found at the basal side of ASP cells, located mostly at the distal ASP tip cells and did not colocalize with any of the endosomal markers examined.
source: Notably, a small number of receptor-ligand puncta were found at the basal side of ASP cells (arrows in Figure 2C,E). They were located mostly at the distal ASP tip cells and did not colocalize with any of the endosomal markers we examined (Figure 2E).
evidence: Figure 2C,E show arrows pointing to basally localized Bnl:GFP-Btl:Cherry puncta that are not in endosomes.

claim: These puncta on the exposed basal side of the ASP might represent Btl:Cherry-bound Bnl:GFP molecules prior to their receptor-mediated endocytosis.
source: These puncta on the exposed basal side of the ASP might represent Btl:Cherry-bound Bnl:GFP molecules prior to their receptor-mediated endocytosis.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the observation that these puncta are receptor-ligand complexes not yet in endosomes, suggesting they represent a pre-endocytosis state.

claim: An αGFP EIF assay identified a distinct steady-state surface-bound extracellular/externalized pool of Bnl:GFP molecules (Bnl:GFPex).
source: An αGFP EIF assay identified a distinct steady-state surface-bound extracellular/externalized pool of Bnl:GFP molecules (Figure 3A; henceforth referred as Bnl:GFPex).
evidence: Figure 3A shows αGFP-based EIF assay detecting externalized Bnl:GFP (red) on ASP surface under detergent-free conditions.

claim: Endogenous levels of EIF-stained Bnl:GFPex puncta appeared to emit very weak GFP-fluorescence, which was rapidly quenched during high magnification (40X) imaging.
source: Interestingly, even though we used a highly sensitive Gallium arsenide phosphide detector for imaging (see Materials and methods), endogenous levels of EIF-stained Bnl:GFPex puncta appeared to emit very weak GFP-fluorescence, which was rapidly quenched during high magnification (40X) imaging.
evidence: This is a direct observation from imaging experiments described in the methods.

claim: This property of GFP-tagged molecules enabled estimation of the levels of externalized/extracellular Bnl:GFP (Bnl:GFPex), distinguishing them from the brightly fluorescent but non-EIF stained intracellular Bnl:GFP puncta in the ASP (Bnl:GFPin).
source: However, this property of GFP-tagged molecules enabled us to estimate the levels of externalized/extracellular Bnl:GFP (Bnl:GFPex), distinguishing them from the brightly fluorescent but non-EIF stained intracellular Bnl:GFP puncta in the ASP (henceforth referred as Bnl:GFPin) (Figure 3A).
evidence: Figure 3A shows distinction between EIF-stained Bnl:GFPex (red) and bright Bnl:GFPin (green) puncta.

claim: Although the EIF-stained Bnl:GFPex molecules represented secreted signals in the extracellular space, they did not disperse randomly in all directions but were asymmetrically localized and only detected on the surfaces of signal producing cells and of the recipient ASP.
source: Most importantly, this experiment showed that although the EIF-stained Bnl:GFPex molecules represented secreted signals in the extracellular space, they did not disperse randomly in all directions. Instead, they were asymmetrically localized and only detected on the surfaces of signal producing cells and of the recipient ASP (Figure 3A,A').
evidence: Figure 3A,A' shows EIF-stained Bnl:GFPex specifically on ASP and source cells, not randomly distributed. Figure 3A' shows intensity gradient plot.

claim: These results showed that Bnl:GFP moved target-specifically in polarized fashion.
source: These results showed that Bnl:GFP moved target-specifically in polarized fashion.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from comparing the asymmetric Bnl:GFPex distribution (Figure 3A) with the random secGFP distribution (Figure 3B).

claim: ASP cells project receptor-containing cytonemes to establish direct membrane contacts with the wing disc Bnl source, and these cytonemes were shown to be essential for induction of pMAPK signaling in the ASP.
source: Previous studies showed that ASP cells project receptor-containing cytonemes to establish direct membrane contacts with the wing disc Bnl source. These cytonemes were shown to be essential for induction of pMAPK signaling in the ASP (Roy et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim cites previous work (Roy et al., 2014) that demonstrated cytoneme contacts and their requirement for signaling.

claim: These nanopuncta were also enriched on the source cells, especially around the bouton-like sites of contact between the cytonemes and the source.
source: These nanopuncta were also enriched on the source cells, especially around the bouton-like sites of contact between the cytonemes and the source (Figure 3F).
evidence: Figure 3F shows nanopuncta enrichment at contact sites between cytonemes and source cells.

claim: An αGFP EIF staining assay in combination with super-resolution imaging showed that these Bnl:GFP nanopuncta included both surface-bound molecules (EIF-stained) and intracellular molecules (non-EIF stained).
source: An αGFP EIF staining assay in combination with super-resolution imaging showed that these Bnl:GFP nanopuncta included both surface-bound molecules (EIF-stained) and intracellular molecules (non-EIF stained) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B,B').
evidence: Figure 3—figure supplement 2B,B' shows αGFP EIF stain (red signal) recognized Bnl:GFP nanopuncta on the cell surface detected by super-resolution imaging.

claim: Native, untagged Bnl could be detected on cytoneme surfaces using the αBnl antibody.
source: Native, untagged Bnl could also be detected on cytoneme surfaces using the αBnl antibody.
evidence: Figure 3G shows αBnl EIF showing biased distribution of native externalized Bnl puncta (Bnlex) in wild type (w-) background on actin-rich structures.

claim: The αBnl EIF assay showed that a high concentration of externalized Bnl (Bnlex) molecules selectively decorate actin-rich ASP cytonemes and the ASP surface of w- wild-type larvae.
source: The αBnl EIF assay showed that a high concentration of externalized Bnl (Bnlex) molecules selectively decorate actin-rich ASP cytonemes and the ASP surface of w- wild-type larvae (Figure 3G).
evidence: Figure 3G shows αBnl EIF showing biased distribution of native externalized Bnl puncta (Bnlex, arrow) in wild type background; grey, phalloidin-Alexa-647.

claim: The distribution of Bnlex was asymmetrical, exactly as observed for Bnl:GFP on CD8:Cherry-marked ASPs.
source: The distribution of Bnlex was asymmetrical, exactly as observed for Bnl:GFP on CD8:Cherry-marked ASPs (Figure 3C).
evidence: Comparison of Figure 3G (native Bnl) with Figure 3C (Bnl:GFP) shows similar asymmetric distribution patterns.

claim: These results suggested that Bnl molecules, irrespective of the presence or absence of fluorescent tags, specifically localize on the surface of the ASP cytonemes for inter-organ transport.
source: These results suggested that Bnl molecules, irrespective of the presence or absence of fluorescent tags, specifically localize on the surface of the ASP cytonemes for inter-organ transport.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from comparing tagged Bnl:GFP (Figure 3C-F) with native Bnl (Figure 3G) showing similar cytoneme localization patterns.

claim: Densely packed Btl:Cherry molecules were visualized on the surface of the ASP cytonemes in btl:cherryendo larvae.
source: Since efficient inter-tissue movement of Bnl molecules along the surface of the recipient cytonemes might require receptor binding, we imaged ASP cytonemes in btl:cherryendo larvae. Densely packed Btl:Cherry molecules were visualized on the surface of the ASP cytonemes (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Figure 3—figure supplement 3A shows endogenous Btl:Cherry marked the ASP cytonemes.

claim: An αBnl-EIF assay in btl:cherryendo larvae showed that the native Bnlex puncta colocalized with the Btl:Cherry puncta on the cytonemes and on ASP surfaces.
source: An αBnl-EIF assay in btl:cherryendo larvae showed that the native Bnlex puncta colocalized with the Btl:Cherry puncta on the cytonemes and on ASP surfaces (Figure 3H).
evidence: Figure 3H shows Bnlex puncta colocalized with endogenous Btl:Cherry on cytonemes extended from the btl:cherryendo ASP.

claim: Receptor-bound Bnl:GFP puncta were observed on cytonemes during live imaging (N = 30).
source: Receptor-bound Bnl:GFP puncta were also observed on cytonemes during live imaging (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B–C'; N = 30).
evidence: Figure 3—figure supplement 3B-C' shows CD8:Cherry-marked or CD4:mIFP-marked cytonemes with colocalized Btl:Cherry and Bnl:GFP puncta (arrow) in live samples.

claim: Bnl is transported by cytonemes from the source to the ASP in a receptor-bound state.
source: Thus, Bnl is transported by cytonemes from the source to the ASP in a receptor-bound state.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from observations showing Bnl colocalization with Btl on cytonemes (Figures 3H, 3—figure supplement 3B-C').

claim: Cytonemes exchange signals by establishing direct physical contacts between the source and recipient cells.
source: Cytonemes exchange signals by establishing direct physical contacts between the source and recipient cells (Chen et al., 2017; González-Méndez et al., 2017; Huang and Kornberg, 2015; Roy et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim cites multiple previous publications demonstrating contact-dependent signaling via cytonemes.

claim: An improved GRASP technique, 'Synaptobrevin-GFP-reconstitution-across-synaptic-partners (syb-GRASP)' revealed multiple functional contact sites between each of the ASP cytonemes and the bnl-source.
source: As shown in Video 3, an improved GRASP technique, 'Synaptobrevin-GFP-reconstitution-across-synaptic-partners (syb-GRASP)' revealed multiple functional contact sites between each of the ASP cytonemes and the bnl-source.
evidence: Video 3 shows cytoneme contact sites marked by sybGRASP, where ASP expressed CD4:GFP11 and wing disc bnl-source expressed syb:GFP1-10.

claim: The actin-rich ASP cytonemes that contacted the disc bnl-source received a significantly higher number of Bnlex puncta in comparison to the non-contacting cytonemes.
source: To estimate the contact-dependency of the cytoneme-mediated Bnl reception, we combined the syb-GRASP experiment with the αBnl EIF assay. This experiment showed that the actin-rich (phalloidin-stained) ASP cytonemes that contacted the disc bnl-source received a significantly higher number of Bnlex puncta in comparison to the non-contacting cytonemes (Figure 3I,I').
evidence: Figure 3I,I' shows comparison of Bnlex (αBnl EIF, red; arrowhead) localization on actin-rich ASP cytonemes (blue, phalloidin) with and without direct contact (green dots, arrow) with disc bnl-source. Graph shows N = 14 ASP; p<0.0001 (two-tailed t-test).

claim: These observations, together with previous reports on the effect of loss of cytoneme contacts on pMAPK signaling in the ASP, provided substantial evidence that cytoneme-mediated Bnl exchange is contact-dependent.
source: These observations, together with the previous reports on the effect of loss of cytoneme contacts on pMAPK signaling in the ASP (Roy et al., 2014), provided substantial evidence that cytoneme-mediated Bnl exchange is contact-dependent.
evidence: This conclusion integrates current data (Figure 3I,I') with previous findings (Roy et al., 2014) on cytoneme-dependent signaling.

claim: Molecular reconstitution of split GFP between ASP cytonemes and source cells suggested that the signaling contacts between the cytoneme and source cell membranes juxtapose within a 20 nm gap distance.
source: Molecular reconstitution of split GFP between ASP cytonemes and source cells suggested that the signaling contacts between the cytoneme and source cell membranes juxtapose within a 20 nm gap distance (Kornberg and Roy, 2014).
evidence: This claim cites previous work (Kornberg and Roy, 2014) that characterized the close proximity of cytoneme-source contacts using GRASP.

claim: Super-resolution images revealed that ASP cytonemes traverse along the surface of the source cells, with each cytoneme establishing contacts with multiple signal-producing cells.
source: To directly visualize and resolve Bnl exchange at these cytoneme contacts, an αBnl EIF assay was combined with super-resolution imaging (see Materials and methods) of the tissues that had both the source and recipient ASP cells marked with distinct membrane-tagged proteins (Figure 3J). The images revealed that ASP cytonemes traverse along the surface of the source cells, with each cytoneme establishing contacts with multiple signal-producing cells.
evidence: Figure 3J shows high-resolution image showing contacts between ASP cytonemes (blue) and wing disc source (green) and enrichment of native externalized Bnl (red; Bnlex, detected with αBnl EIF) at these contact points.

claim: Although the producing cells occupy a large area, the externalized Bnl proteins were specifically enriched at the cytoneme contact sites.
source: Although the producing cells occupy a large area, the externalized Bnl proteins were specifically enriched at the cytoneme contact sites.
evidence: Figure 3J shows selective enrichment of Bnl at contact sites rather than uniform distribution across source cells.

claim: This observation suggests that the producing cells selectively release Bnl at these contact sites.
source: This observation suggests that the producing cells selectively release Bnl at these contact sites.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observation that Bnl is enriched at contact sites (Figure 3J).

claim: These ASP cytonemes also localized Bnlex puncta on their shafts, suggesting that the signal might be transported from the contact sites to the ASP along the surface of the cytonemes.
source: These ASP cytonemes also localized Bnlex puncta on their shafts, suggesting that the signal might be transported from the contact sites to the ASP along the surface of the cytonemes.
evidence: Figure 3J shows Bnl distribution along cytoneme shafts, suggesting transport mechanism.

claim: A similar retrograde movement of Dpp was previously observed through ASP cytonemes.
source: A similar retrograde movement of Dpp was previously observed through ASP cytonemes (Roy et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim cites previous work (Roy et al., 2014) showing retrograde transport of another morphogen (Dpp) via cytonemes.

claim: Knockdown of cytoneme-regulator genes (diaphanous, neuroglian, singed) in clones of cells significantly decreased Bnl:GFP levels in the mutant cells, but not in the neighboring WT cells.
source: However, knockdown of cytoneme-regulator genes in clones of cells significantly decreased Bnl:GFP levels in the mutant cells, but not in the neighboring WT cells (Figure 4B–E; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Figure 4B-D shows representative images of Bnl:GFP uptake in CD4:mIFP-marked clones expressing snRNAi, diaRNAi, or nrgRNAi. Figure 4E shows box plot comparing ratios with statistical significance (p<0.05, p<0.01, p<0.001).

claim: The ratio of Bnl:GFP concentration outside (WT area) to inside (cytoneme deficient) of the mutant clones increased significantly compared to the WT control condition.
source: Consequently, the ratio of Bnl:GFP concentration outside (WT area) to inside (cytoneme deficient) of the mutant clones increased significantly compared to the WT control condition (Figure 4E).
evidence: Figure 4E shows box plot with statistical analysis (two-tailed t-test) demonstrating significant increase in outside/inside ratio for cytoneme-deficient mutants.

claim: These results showed that cytonemes are essential for the ASP cells to receive Bnl:GFP from the wing disc source.
source: These results showed that cytonemes are essential for the ASP cells to receive Bnl:GFP from the wing disc source.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the clonal analysis showing reduced Bnl:GFP uptake in cytoneme-deficient clones (Figure 4A-E).

claim: RNAi-mediated knockdown of btl in clones of ASP cells led to a significant reduction of Bnl:GFPex on the mutant clonal areas compared to the WT neighboring cells.
source: Indeed, RNAi-mediated knockdown of btl in clones of ASP cells led to a significant reduction of Bnl:GFPex on the mutant clonal areas compared to the WT neighboring cells (Figure 4G,G').
evidence: Figure 4G shows representative image of αGFP EIF stained Bnl:GFPex (red) in CD4:mIFP-marked (blue) btl LOF (btlRNAi) clone. Figure 4G' shows plot comparing relative Bnl:GFPex density inside versus outside of btl LOF clones (N = 3 independent ASPs) with p value from two-tailed t-test.

claim: The distribution pattern of Bnl:GFPex was consistent with a cytoneme-dependent mechanism of gradient formation.
source: Clearly, the distribution pattern of Bnl:GFPex was consistent with a cytoneme-dependent mechanism of gradient formation.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from comparing observed distribution pattern (Figure 4G) with predicted patterns for cytoneme-dependent versus diffusion-based mechanisms (Figure 4F,F').

claim: In the ASP stalk, where normal levels of Btl are low, generation of btl overexpressing (btl-GOF) clones induced extension of long polarized cytonemes that projected toward the underlying disc bnl-source.
source: Furthermore, in the ASP stalk, where normal levels of Btl are low, generation of btl overexpressing (btl-GOF, gain of function) clones induced extension of long polarized cytonemes that projected toward the underlying disc bnl-source.
evidence: Figure 4H,H' shows representative image showing enrichment of αGFP EIF stained Bnl:GFPex (red) on long cytonemes (arrow) projected from btlGOF clones in the ASP stalk.

claim: These cytonemes from btl-GOF clones were enriched with EIF-stained Bnl:GFPex on their surfaces and the mutant clones had a higher concentration of Bnl:GFPex than their neighbors.
source: These cytonemes were enriched with EIF-stained Bnl:GFPex on their surfaces (Figure 4H,H') and the mutant clones had a higher concentration of Bnl:GFPex than their neighbors (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Figure 4H,H' shows Bnl:GFPex enrichment on cytonemes from btl-GOF clones. Figure 4—figure supplement 1B shows bar graphs comparing relative Bnl:GFPex density inside versus outside of four different btl GOF clones.

claim: This result provided direct evidence that the induction of cytonemes in ASP cells increased cell-autonomous contact-dependent Bnl:GFP uptake.
source: This result provided direct evidence that the induction of cytonemes in ASP cells increased cell-autonomous contact-dependent Bnl:GFP uptake.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the btl-GOF experiment showing increased cytonemes correlate with increased Bnl:GFP uptake (Figure 4H,H', Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).

claim: Long oriented cytonemes that could establish contacts with the Bnl source were produced in a graded fashion across the length of the ASP.
source: Thus, long oriented cytonemes that could establish contacts with the Bnl source were produced in a graded fashion across the length of the ASP.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the quantitative analysis of cytoneme numbers and orientations from different ASP regions (Figure 5A-D'').

claim: A similar gradient in the number of signaling contacts was also observed from cytonemes produced across the vertical axis of the tubular tissue, with ASP cells in the lower layer proximal to the bnl-source having a higher frequency of cytoneme contacts compared to the upper cell layer.
source: A similar gradient in the number of signaling contacts was also observed from cytonemes produced across the vertical axis of the tubular tissue. In a syb-GRASP experiment between the disc and ASP, ASP cells in the lower layer that is proximal to the bnl-source had a higher frequency of cytoneme contacts compared to the upper cell layer (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B; Videos 3, 4 and 5).
evidence: Figure 5—figure supplement 1B shows frequency of cytoneme-mediated contacts established by upper and lower layers of the ASP with the bnl-source. Videos 3, 4, and 5 show 3D visualization of contacts.

claim: These results suggested that differential levels of signal uptake through a graded number of cytonemes give rise to the tissue-specific shapes of the Bnl:GFP gradient.
source: These results suggested that differential levels of signal uptake through a graded number of cytonemes give rise to the tissue-specific shapes of the Bnl:GFP gradient.
evidence: This conclusion integrates observations of graded cytoneme numbers (Figure 5) with graded Bnl:GFP distribution (Figure 1).

claim: ASP cells within a three-cell diameter domain from the distal tip along the D-P axis, which received the highest concentration of Bnl:GFP, expressed sty.
source: We found that ASP cells within a three-cell diameter domain from the distal tip along the D-P axis, which received the highest concentration of Bnl:GFP, expressed sty (Figure 6A,E; Figure 6—figure supplement 1A; Figure 6—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: Figure 6A shows correlation of Bnl:GFP gradient with sty-lacZ expression domain. Figure 6E shows drawing depicting sty expression within 1st-3rd cells from distal tip. Figure 6—figure supplement 1A shows quantitative data. Figure 6—figure supplement 2A,B show additional examples.

claim: A broader zone of ~6–7 cell-diameters from the tip along the D-P axis received high-to-moderate levels of Bnl:GFP and induced pntP1.
source: A broader zone of ~6–7 cell-diameters from the tip along the D-P axis received high-to-moderate levels of Bnl:GFP and induced pntP1 (Figure 6B,E; Figure 6—figure supplement 1A; Figure 6—figure supplement 2C, D).
evidence: Figure 6B shows correlation of Bnl:GFP gradient with pntP1-lacZ expression. Figure 6E shows pntP1 expression within 1st-7th cells. Figure 6—figure supplement 1A shows quantitative data. Figure 6—figure supplement 2C,D show additional examples.

claim: In the proximal stalk of the ASP from the 7th to 12th cell away from the tip along the D-P axis, which received negligible levels of Bnl:GFP, cut and yan expression gradually increased with increasing distance from the source.
source: In contrast, the proximal stalk of the ASP from the 7th to 12th cell away from the tip along the D-P axis received negligible levels of Bnl:GFP. In this ASP domain, cut and yan expression gradually increased with increasing distance from the source (Figure 6C–E; Figure 6—figure supplement 1A; Figure 6—figure supplement 2E-H).
evidence: Figure 6C,D show correlation of Bnl:GFP gradient with cut and yan expression domains. Figure 6E shows cut expression in 7th-14th cells and yan in 11th-14th cells. Figure 6—figure supplement 1A shows quantitative data. Figure 6—figure supplement 2E-H show additional examples.

claim: The gradients of cut and yan expression had the exact opposite pattern as the pntP1 and Bnl:GFP gradients.
source: Thus, the gradients of cut and yan expression had the exact opposite pattern as the pntP1 and Bnl:GFP gradients.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from comparing the spatial expression domains shown in Figure 6A-E.

claim: Across the recipient ASP epithelium, high levels of Bnl:GFP correlated with sty expression, and gradually decreasing levels of Bnl:GFP further away from the source correlated with the expression zones of pntP1, cut, and yan, respectively.
source: Thus, across the recipient ASP epithelium, high levels of Bnl:GFP correlated with sty expression, and gradually decreasing levels of Bnl:GFP further away from the source correlated with the expression zones of pntP1, cut, and yan, respectively (Figure 6E,F).
evidence: Figure 6E,F show drawings summarizing the spatial correlation of Bnl:GFP levels with target gene expression domains.

claim: Similar spatial patterning in the gene-expression zones of sty and different ETS family proteins is known to be induced by the vertebrate FGF8 morphogen in mouse neuroectoderm.
source: Similar spatial patterning in the gene-expression zones of sty and different ETS family proteins is known to be induced by the vertebrate FGF8 morphogen in mouse neuroectoderm (Toyoda et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim cites previous work (Toyoda et al., 2010) showing similar concentration-dependent gene expression patterns induced by vertebrate FGF8.

claim: Even while highly expressed from the wing disc source, Bnl:GFP moved only target-specifically from the disc source to the ASP.
source: Remarkably, even while highly expressed from the wing disc source, Bnl:GFP moved only target-specifically from the disc source to the ASP (Figure 6H,H').
evidence: Figure 6H,H' shows overexpression of Bnl:GFP from disc bnl-source (arrowhead) expanded the range of Bnl:GFP and pMAPK signaling to the ASP stalk, but signal remained specific to ASP.

claim: The spatial range of the overexpressed signal and the signaling expanded to all parts of the ASP, including the stalk.
source: In comparison to the normal range of endogenous Bnl:GFP distribution and Bnl (pMAPK) signaling (Figure 6G), the spatial range of the overexpressed signal and the signaling expanded to all parts of the ASP, including the stalk (Figure 6H).
evidence: Figure 6H shows expanded range of Bnl:GFP and pMAPK signaling (α-dpERK, blue) to ASP stalk upon overexpression, compared to normal range in Figure 6G.

claim: The expanded range of signal led to retraction of the Cut and Yan expressing zone from within the stalk to only the farthest region in the TC, which received little or no Bnl:GFP from the disc source.
source: The expanded range of signal led to retraction of the Cut and Yan expressing zone from within the stalk to only the farthest region in the TC, which received little or no Bnl:GFP from the disc source (Figure 6H–I).
evidence: Figure 6H,I show suppression/retraction of cut (H, arrow) and yan (I, arrow) domains to the farthest part that received little or no Bnl:GFP upon Bnl overexpression.

claim: Ectopic clones of either Bnl:GFP or Bnl in the ASP stalk non-autonomously induced sty and pntP1 and suppressed cut in the surrounding cells.
source: Moreover, ectopic clones of either Bnl:GFP or Bnl in the ASP stalk non-autonomously induced sty and pntP1 and suppressed cut in the surrounding cells (Figure 6J,K,L; Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Figure 6K,L show small Bnl:GFP overexpressing clones (green) at ASP stalk non-autonomously induced pntP1 (K; red; arrow) and suppressed cut (L; red; arrow). Figure 6—figure supplement 1D shows similar results for sty induction.

claim: These results showed that Bnl acts as a morphogen to induce concentration-dependent expression of different genes.
source: These results showed that Bnl acts as a morphogen to induce concentration-dependent expression of different genes.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from experiments showing differential gene induction at different Bnl concentrations (Figure 6A-L).

claim: It was previously reported that PntP1 and Yan antagonize each other's expression.
source: It was previously reported that PntP1 and Yan antagonize each other's expression (Ohshiro et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim cites previous work (Ohshiro et al., 2002) showing reciprocal antagonism between PntP1 and Yan.

claim: Reduction of PntP1 levels in the mutant pntP1 LOF (pntP1 RNAi) clones in the ASP tip autonomously upregulated Cut expression within the clones.
source: Reduction of PntP1 levels in the mutant pntP1 LOF (pntP1 RNAi) clones in the ASP tip autonomously upregulated Cut expression within the clones, whereas overexpression of PntP1 in the ectopic pntP1 GOF clones in the ASP stalk suppressed cut in the mutant cells (Figure 6M,N).
evidence: Figure 6M shows pntP1 LOF clone (CD8:GFP) in ASP tip/mid-region with upregulated Cut (red). Figure 6N shows pntP1 GOF clone in ASP stalk/TC region with suppressed Cut.

claim: Overexpression of PntP1 in the ectopic pntP1 GOF clones in the ASP stalk suppressed cut in the mutant cells.
source: Reduction of PntP1 levels in the mutant pntP1 LOF (pntP1 RNAi) clones in the ASP tip autonomously upregulated Cut expression within the clones, whereas overexpression of PntP1 in the ectopic pntP1 GOF clones in the ASP stalk suppressed cut in the mutant cells (Figure 6M,N).
evidence: Figure 6N shows pntP1 GOF clone in ASP stalk/TC region with suppressed Cut (red).

claim: Ectopic cut GOF clones in the ASP tip suppressed pntP1 and cut LOF clones (cut RNAi) in the proximal ASP stalk induced pntP1 within the mutant cells.
source: On the other hand, ectopic cut GOF clones in the ASP tip suppressed pntP1 and cut LOF clones (cut RNAi) in the proximal ASP stalk induced pntP1 within the mutant cells (Figure 6O,P).
evidence: Figure 6O shows cut GOF clone in ASP tip/mid-region suppressed pntP1 (red, pntP1-lacZ). Figure 6P shows cut LOF clone in ASP stalk/TC region induced pntP1 (red).

claim: PntP1 and Cut reciprocally inhibit each other's expression.
source: Thus, PntP1 and Cut reciprocally inhibit each other's expression.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the reciprocal effects shown in Figure 6M-P.

claim: Although PntP1 is a known inducer of btl, pntP1 GOF/LOF clones showed only cell-autonomous effects on cut.
source: Notably, although PntP1 is a known inducer of btl, pntP1 GOF/LOF clones showed only cell-autonomous effects on cut.
evidence: This observation is noted in the text and shown in Figure 6M-P where effects are restricted to clone boundaries.

claim: The btl GOF clones in the ASP showed a similar autonomous signaling effect.
source: The btl GOF clones in the ASP showed a similar autonomous signaling effect (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Figure 6—figure supplement 1E shows Btl overexpression clones (white, pseudocolored) induced dpERK (red) signaling autonomously.

claim: Each Bnl:GFP GOF clone in the ASP induced non-autonomous effects and organized the surrounding cells to form a new branch (N = 35).
source: In contrast, each Bnl:GFP GOF clone in the ASP induced non-autonomous effects and organized the surrounding cells to form a new branch (N = 35; Figure 6K,L).
evidence: Figure 6K,L show small Bnl:GFP overexpressing clones (green) at ASP stalk non-autonomously organized surrounding cells to induce ectopic branch (dashed outlines). N = 35 samples examined.

claim: All these results provided evidence that Bnl acts as a classical morphogen to induce sty at a high level and pntP1, cut, and yan gradually at lower levels in the ASP.
source: All these results provided evidence that Bnl acts as a classical morphogen to induce sty at a high level and pntP1, cut, and yan gradually at lower levels in the ASP (Figure 6E,F).
evidence: This conclusion integrates all observations from Figure 6 showing concentration-dependent gene induction.

claim: When ectopic cut GOF clones were induced in the distal tip/mid-ASP regions, the mutant cells produced significantly fewer long and oriented cytonemes compared to the wt clones at an equivalent position.
source: When we induced ectopic cut GOF clones in the distal tip/mid-ASP regions, the mutant cells produced significantly fewer long and oriented cytonemes compared to the wt clones at an equivalent position (Figure 7A,A' versus Figure 5A'',C).
evidence: Figure 7A,A' show CD8:GFP-marked cut-GOF clones at ASP tip suppressed long oriented cytoneme formation with rose plots showing number and orientation of cytonemes. Comparison with control in Figure 5A'',C shows significant reduction.

claim: This cytoneme deficiency in the cut GOF clones correlated with the autonomous reduction of Bnl:GFP uptake in the mutant clones from the mid/tip of the ASP.
source: This cytoneme deficiency in the cut GOF clones correlated with the autonomous reduction of Bnl:GFP uptake in the mutant clones from the mid/tip of the ASP (Figure 7A–B').
evidence: Figure 7B,B' show cut-GOF clone (red, CD4:mIFP) suppressed Bnl:GFP uptake cell-autonomously with graph comparing Bnl:GFP concentration in cut-GOF clones and corresponding neighboring control area (N = 6); p value from two-tailed t-test.

claim: The orientation and number of cytonemes from the ASP stalk cells, which generally had high levels of Cut and produced randomly oriented short cytonemes, remained unaffected by cut GOF.
source: On the other hand, the orientation and number of cytonemes from the ASP stalk cells, which generally had high levels of Cut and produced randomly oriented short cytonemes, remained unaffected by cut GOF (Figure 7A').
evidence: Figure 7A' shows rose plots for cut GOF clones in proximal stalk showing similar cytoneme patterns as control.

claim: High levels of Cut negatively regulate the formation of cytonemes that orient specifically toward the bnl-source.
source: Thus, high levels of Cut negatively regulate the formation of cytonemes that orient specifically toward the bnl-source.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the cut GOF experiments showing reduced oriented cytonemes in tip cells but not stalk cells (Figure 7A,A').

claim: Cut was also known to be a suppressor of btl in the larval spiracular branch.
source: In addition to this finding, Cut was also known to be a suppressor of btl in the larval spiracular branch (Pitsouli and Perrimon, 2013).
evidence: This claim cites previous work (Pitsouli and Perrimon, 2013) showing Cut suppresses btl expression.

claim: High levels of Cut elicit negative feedback on Bnl signaling by suppressing both the Bnl-receiving cytonemes and Btl synthesis.
source: Therefore, high levels of Cut elicit negative feedback on Bnl signaling by suppressing both the Bnl-receiving cytonemes and Btl synthesis (Figure 8A,A').
evidence: This conclusion integrates current findings on cytoneme suppression (Figure 7A-B') with previous knowledge of btl suppression (Pitsouli and Perrimon, 2013). Figure 8A,A' shows model incorporating this negative feedback.

claim: A similar inhibitory effect on cytonemes was observed for Yan, which was a known antagonist for PntP1 and embryonic tracheal filopodia formation.
source: A similar inhibitory effect on cytonemes was observed for Yan, which was a known antagonist for PntP1 and embryonic tracheal filopodia formation (Okenve-Ramos and Llimargas, 2014) (Figure 7—supplement figure 1A-B'; Figure 8A').
evidence: Figure 7—figure supplement 1A-B' show examples of cytonemes from CD8:GFP-marked yan GOF clones at tip and stalk with respective R-plots. Citation to Okenve-Ramos and Llimargas, 2014 supports known role of Yan.

claim: These results showed that cut and yan, the two genes that are expressed in the ASP stalk in response to lower Bnl levels, suppress cytoneme-formation and Btl expression.
source: Collectively, these results showed that cut and yan, the two genes that are expressed in the ASP stalk in response to lower Bnl levels, suppress cytoneme-formation and Btl expression.
evidence: This conclusion integrates findings on Cut (Figure 7A-B') and Yan (Figure 7—figure supplement 1) effects on cytonemes with their expression patterns (Figure 6C-E).

claim: When ectopic pntP1 GOF clones were generated in the ASP stalk, the mutant cells extended significantly more long (>30 μm) cytonemes oriented toward the underlying disc bnl-source than the WT clones.
source: When ectopic pntP1 GOF clones were generated in the ASP stalk, the mutant cells extended significantly more long (>30 μm) cytonemes oriented toward the underlying disc bnl-source than the WT clones (Figure 7C,C', compared to Figure 5A,C).
evidence: Figure 7C,C' show pntP1-GOF clones induced long oriented cytonemes at ASP stalk with rose plots showing number and orientation of cytonemes of different lengths from proximal (N = 5) and distal tip (N = 8) clones. Comparison with control in Figure 5A,C shows significant increase.

claim: pntP1-LOF clones at the ASP tip extended a significantly fewer number of long oriented cytonemes from the tip cells than the WT clones.
source: In contrast, pntP1-LOF clones at the ASP tip extended a significantly fewer number of long oriented cytonemes from the tip cells than the WT clones (Figure 7D,D', compared to Figure 5A'',C).
evidence: Figure 7D,D' show pntP1-LOF clones suppressed long oriented cytonemes at ASP tip with rose plots showing number and orientation. Comparison with control in Figure 5A'',C shows significant reduction.

claim: Loss of cytonemes in the pntP1 LOF clones correlated with the suppression of Bnl:GFP uptake in the mutant ASP cells.
source: Loss of cytonemes in the pntP1 LOF clones correlated with the suppression of Bnl:GFP uptake in the mutant ASP cells, and an increase in the number of cytonemes in the pntP1 GOF cells increased the levels of Bnl:GFP in them (Figure 7E–H).
evidence: Figure 7E,E' show CD4:mIFP-marked pntP1-LOF clone at ASP tip suppressed Bnl:GFP uptake with plot comparing uptake in clone versus neighboring control area (N = 4). Figure 7F-H show pntP1 GOF clones in ASP stalk had higher levels of Bnl:GFP.

claim: An increase in the number of cytonemes in the pntP1 GOF cells increased the levels of Bnl:GFP in them.
source: Loss of cytonemes in the pntP1 LOF clones correlated with the suppression of Bnl:GFP uptake in the mutant ASP cells, and an increase in the number of cytonemes in the pntP1 GOF cells increased the levels of Bnl:GFP in them (Figure 7E–H).
evidence: Figure 7F shows pnt-P1 GOF clones in ASP stalk showed higher levels of Bnl:GFP in clones compared to WT neighboring area. Figure 7H shows graph of fold difference of Bnl:GFP and Bnl:GFPex density inside to outside of pntP1 GOF clones (N = 5 each).

claim: An αGFP EIF assay revealed that the long cytonemes projecting from the pntP1 GOF clones in the ASP stalk were enriched in EIF-stained Bnl:GFPex, suggesting that the cells received signal by extending cytonemes.
source: An αGFP EIF assay revealed that the long cytonemes projecting from the pntP1 GOF clones in the ASP stalk were enriched in EIF-stained Bnl:GFPex, suggesting that the cells received signal by extending cytonemes (Figure 7G,H).
evidence: Figure 7G shows αGFP EIF showed high Bnl:GFPex on cytonemes and clonal cell body on pnt-P1 GOF clones in ASP stalk. Figure 7H shows quantification.

claim: PntP1 was known to induce btl transcription in embryonic trachea.
source: In addition, PntP1 was known to induce btl transcription in embryonic trachea (Ohshiro et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim cites previous work (Ohshiro et al., 2002) showing PntP1 induces btl transcription.

claim: When small (1–4 cells) pntP1 GOF clones were generated in the stalk of the ASP in btl:cherryendo larvae, the PntP1 overexpression increased the levels of Btl:Cherry in the clones.
source: When we generated small (1–4 cells) pntP1 GOF clones in the stalk of the ASP in btl:cherryendo larvae, the PntP1 overexpression increased the levels of Btl:Cherry in the clones.
evidence: Figure 7I shows pntP1 GOF clones induced btl:cherryendo expression.

claim: The newly synthesized Btl:Cherry molecules also formed local concentration gradients within each of the pntP1 GOF clones.
source: Strikingly, the newly synthesized Btl:Cherry molecules also formed local concentration gradients within each of the pntP1 GOF clones (Figure 7I).
evidence: Figure 7I shows pntP1 GOF clones induced btl:cherryendo expression and polarized graded organization of Btl:Cherry molecules.

claim: These results showed that PntP1 elicits positive-feedback on Btl synthesis and Bnl-receiving cytoneme production.
source: These results showed that PntP1 elicits positive-feedback on Btl synthesis and Bnl-receiving cytoneme production (Figure 8A').
evidence: This conclusion integrates findings on PntP1 effects on cytonemes (Figure 7C-H) and Btl expression (Figure 7I). Figure 8A' shows model incorporating this positive feedback.

claim: PntP1 and Cut or PntP1 and Yan can reciprocally inhibit each other's expression.
source: Interestingly, PntP1 and Cut (Figure 6M–P) or PntP1 and Yan (Ohshiro et al., 2002) can reciprocally inhibit each other's expression.
evidence: Figure 6M-P shows reciprocal inhibition between PntP1 and Cut. Citation to Ohshiro et al., 2002 supports reciprocal inhibition between PntP1 and Yan.

claim: A ratio of the levels of PntP1 to Cut or to Yan could determine the number of cytonemes and Btl receptors in a cell.
source: Therefore, a ratio of the levels of PntP1 to Cut or to Yan could determine the number of cytonemes and Btl receptors in a cell.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the reciprocal inhibition between PntP1 and Cut/Yan (Figure 6M-P, Ohshiro et al., 2002) and their opposite effects on cytonemes (Figure 7).

claim: The counteracting activities of PntP1 and Cut/Yan and their expression from two opposite poles in response to the high-to-low Bnl levels in the ASP establish a steady-state gradient of numbers of Btl-containing cytonemes.
source: Based on our results, we propose that the counteracting activities of PntP1 and Cut/Yan and their expression from two opposite poles in response to the high-to-low Bnl levels in the ASP establish a steady-state gradient of numbers of Btl-containing cytonemes.
evidence: This is a proposed model integrating all findings on PntP1 and Cut/Yan expression patterns (Figure 6) and their effects on cytonemes (Figure 7).

claim: Signaling through these cytonemes would self-generate the shape of a robust signal and signaling gradient.
source: Signaling through these cytonemes would self-generate the shape of a robust signal and signaling gradient (Figure 8A').
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism shown in the model in Figure 8A' integrating all findings.

claim: Prior to this study, branching morphogenesis of tissues such as vertebrate lung or vasculature was proposed to be induced by exogenous, diffusible signal gradients.
source: Prior to this study, branching morphogenesis of tissues such as vertebrate lung or vasculature was proposed to be induced by exogenous, diffusible signal gradients.
evidence: This statement describes the prevailing model before this study, providing context for the significance of the findings.

claim: A mesenchymal FGF10 gradient induces branching in the vertebrate lung, and a Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor/VEGF gradient induces vascular sprouting.
source: For instance, a mesenchymal FGF10 gradient induces branching in the vertebrate lung, and a Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor/VEGF gradient induces vascular sprouting (Affolter et al., 2009; Spurlin and Nelson, 2017).
evidence: This claim cites previous work (Affolter et al., 2009; Spurlin and Nelson, 2017) describing roles of FGF10 and VEGF gradients in branching morphogenesis.

claim: This demonstration and detailed characterization of the Bnl gradient represents the first example of an inductive gradient for branching morphogenesis.
source: Although the paracrine functions of these signals were well characterized, our demonstration and detailed characterization of the Bnl gradient represents the first example of an inductive gradient for branching morphogenesis.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty and significance of the current study's findings.

claim: In contrast to the traditional idea of a preexisting diffusible gradient, the shapes of the inductive Bnl gradient are dynamic, adaptable, and form only in a receptor-bound state within the recipient tissue.
source: In contrast to the traditional idea of a preexisting diffusible gradient, we showed that the shapes of the inductive Bnl gradient are dynamic, adaptable, and form only in a receptor-bound state within the recipient tissue.
evidence: This conclusion summarizes key findings from Figures 1-2 showing dynamic gradient formation coordinated with ASP growth and receptor-bound Bnl distribution.

claim: The Bnl gradient self-generates its variable recipient branch-specific shapes by regulating its cytoneme-mediated transport.
source: Moreover, we showed that the Bnl gradient self-generates its variable recipient branch-specific shapes by regulating its cytoneme-mediated transport.
evidence: This conclusion summarizes key findings from Figures 5-7 showing feedback regulation of cytoneme formation by Bnl target genes.

claim: Self-generation of tissue-specific gradients may be a common and essential strategy for sustaining the robust, yet variable gradient shapes in dynamically migrating tissues.
source: Self-generation of tissue-specific gradients may be a common and essential strategy for sustaining the robust, yet variable gradient shapes in dynamically migrating tissues.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the broader implications of the findings.

claim: The chemokine Cxcl12a also forms a self-generating gradient to regulate dynamic migration of the Zebrafish lateral line.
source: Consistent with this view, the chemokine Cxcl12a also forms a self-generating gradient to regulate dynamic migration of the Zebrafish lateral line (Donà et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim cites previous work (Donà et al., 2013) showing another example of self-generating gradient.

claim: Inductive signals such as Bnl or VEGF were previously thought to induce chemotactic migration by inducing binary signaling responses in the recipient cells.
source: Notably, inductive signals such as Bnl or VEGF were previously thought to induce chemotactic migration by inducing binary signaling responses in the recipient cells (Ochoa-Espinosa and Affolter, 2012).
evidence: This claim cites previous work (Ochoa-Espinosa and Affolter, 2012) describing the traditional view of Bnl/VEGF function.

claim: Identification of an organizer-like morphogenetic role of Bnl brings a critical shift to our understanding of branching morphogenesis.
source: Therefore, identification of an organizer-like morphogenetic role of Bnl brings a critical shift to our understanding of branching morphogenesis.
evidence: This is a claim about the significance of the findings showing Bnl acts as a morphogen rather than a simple chemoattractant.

claim: Several earlier reports, including biophysical analyses of vertebrate FGF8 and its distribution patterns in tissues, proposed a free or restricted diffusion-based dispersion mechanism for gradient formation.
source: Several earlier reports, including biophysical analyses of vertebrate FGF8 and its distribution patterns in tissues, proposed a free or restricted diffusion-based dispersion mechanism for gradient formation (Bökel and Brand, 2013; Toyoda et al., 2010; Yu et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim cites previous work (Bökel and Brand, 2013; Toyoda et al., 2010; Yu et al., 2009) proposing diffusion-based mechanisms for FGF gradient formation.

claim: An alternative model proposed that the FGF8 morphogen gradient is also formed by gradual decay of fgf8 mRNA and its translation in a growing vertebrate embryo.
source: An alternative model proposed that the FGF8 morphogen gradient is also formed by gradual decay of fgf8 mRNA and its translation in a growing vertebrate embryo (Dubrulle and Pourquié, 2004).
evidence: This claim cites previous work (Dubrulle and Pourquié, 2004) proposing an mRNA decay-based mechanism for FGF8 gradient formation.

claim: In contrast, all genetic analyses and direct imaging results show that the Bnl gradient is formed by cytoneme-mediated direct transport.
source: In contrast, all of our genetic analyses and direct imaging results show that the Bnl gradient is formed by cytoneme-mediated direct transport.
evidence: This conclusion summarizes findings from Figures 3-4 showing cytoneme-dependent Bnl transport and gradient formation.

claim: An earlier study showed that ASP cells project Btl-containing cytonemes to establish contact with the disc Bnl source, and fail to induce pMAPK signaling without these cytoneme-mediated contacts.
source: An earlier study showed that ASP cells project Btl-containing cytonemes to establish contact with the disc Bnl source, and fail to induce pMAPK signaling without these cytoneme-mediated contacts (Roy et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim cites previous work (Roy et al., 2014) that first demonstrated cytoneme-dependent signaling in this system.

claim: By generating endo-tagged Bnl:GFP and Btl:Cherry constructs expressed at physiological levels, utilizing an EIF assay to detect externalized Bnl molecules, and by applying high resolution visualization techniques, reliable and unbiased evidence for Bnl dispersion via cytonemes was obtained.
source: By generating endo-tagged Bnl:GFP and Btl:Cherry constructs expressed at physiological levels, utilizing an EIF assay to detect externalized Bnl molecules, and by applying high resolution visualization techniques, we obtained reliable and unbiased evidence for Bnl dispersion via cytonemes.
evidence: This statement summarizes the methodological approaches used in the study (Figures 1-3) and their contribution to the findings.

claim: ASP cytonemes receive Bnl molecules by establishing direct membrane synapses with the signal producing cells.
source: We showed that ASP cytonemes receive Bnl molecules by establishing direct membrane synapses with the signal producing cells.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from syb-GRASP experiments (Figure 3I-J, Videos 3-5) and EIF assays (Figure 3C-H) showing contact-dependent Bnl reception.

claim: Super-resolution imaging of membrane-marked ASP and source cells documented these synaptic sites and showed a selective enrichment of externalized Bnl molecules only at these signaling contacts.
source: Super-resolution imaging of membrane-marked ASP and source cells documented these synaptic sites and showed a selective enrichment of externalized Bnl molecules only at these signaling contacts (Figure 3J).
evidence: Figure 3J shows high-resolution image of contacts between ASP cytonemes and wing disc source with enrichment of Bnl at contact points.

claim: At this point, we do not know why and how Bnl is released from producing cells only at cytoneme-source membrane contact sites.
source: At this point, we do not know why and how Bnl is released from producing cells only at cytoneme-source membrane contact sites.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a gap in understanding despite the observations.

claim: Understanding the mechanisms underlying this process is an important new direction for future investigations.
source: Understanding the mechanisms underlying this process is an important new direction for future investigations.
evidence: This is a statement about future research directions.

claim: Antibody-based EIF analysis under detergent-free conditions and super-resolution imaging of endogenously expressed Bnl:GFP showed that at a steady state, a high concentration of the signal moves along the surface of the cytonemes in receptor-bound forms.
source: Antibody-based EIF analysis under detergent-free conditions and super-resolution imaging of endogenously expressed Bnl:GFP showed that at a steady state, a high concentration of the signal moves along the surface of the cytonemes in receptor-bound forms (Figure 3C–H).
evidence: Figure 3C-H shows EIF assays and super-resolution imaging demonstrating Bnl localization on cytoneme surfaces in receptor-bound form.

claim: It is likely that receptor-bound Bnl ligands move along the surface of the cytonemes by an energy-dependent motor transport and are endocytosed when they reach the ASP cell body.
source: It is likely that receptor-bound Bnl ligands move along the surface of the cytonemes by an energy-dependent motor transport and are endocytosed when they reach the ASP cell body.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the mechanism of Bnl transport along cytonemes based on observations.

claim: Super-resolution imaging revealed a previously uncharacterized sub-resolution distribution of Bnl:GFP nanopuncta, suggesting the existence of novel cellular and molecular events that regulate the cytoneme-mediated signaling process.
source: Super-resolution imaging also revealed a previously uncharacterized sub-resolution distribution of Bnl:GFP nanopuncta (Figure 3F–F''; Figure 3—supplement figure 2), suggesting the existence of novel cellular and molecular events that regulate the cytoneme-mediated signaling process.
evidence: Figure 3F-F'' and Figure 3—figure supplement 2 show super-resolution images revealing nanopuncta. The suggestion of novel mechanisms is speculative.

claim: Each of these individual cellular and molecular mechanisms would influence the levels of Bnl signaling in a cell and thereby would contribute to the essential feedback mechanisms by which the cytoneme and the morphogen gradients are formed.
source: Each of these individual cellular and molecular mechanisms would influence the levels of Bnl signaling in a cell and thereby would contribute to the essential feedback mechanisms by which the cytoneme and the morphogen gradients are formed.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about how various mechanisms might contribute to gradient formation.

claim: Contact-dependent Bnl exchange implies that the ASP cells can interpret the direction from where (and from whom) they receive the Bnl signal, in addition to its levels.
source: Contact-dependent Bnl exchange implies that the ASP cells can interpret the direction from where (and from whom) they receive the Bnl signal, in addition to its levels.
evidence: This is an inference based on the contact-dependent nature of Bnl exchange shown in Figure 3I,I'.

claim: We do not know how ASP cytonemes find the bnl-source and establish the signaling contacts.
source: We do not know how ASP cytonemes find the bnl-source and establish the signaling contacts.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a gap in understanding.

claim: A recent study had shown an important regulatory role of the components of the extracellular matrix, which interact with the signal-specific cytonemes and stabilize their directionality.
source: A recent study had shown an important regulatory role of the components of the extracellular matrix, which interact with the signal-specific cytonemes and stabilize their directionality (Huang and Kornberg, 2016).
evidence: This claim cites previous work (Huang and Kornberg, 2016) showing ECM role in cytoneme guidance.

claim: Another possible mechanism could be that the cells in the disc Bnl source extend Bnl-containing cytonemes to establish an initial contact with the recipient cytonemes to provide them the necessary pathfinding information.
source: Another possible mechanism could be that the cells in the disc Bnl source extend Bnl-containing cytonemes to establish an initial contact with the recipient cytonemes to provide them the necessary pathfinding information.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about a possible mechanism for cytoneme guidance.

claim: Hh is known to be delivered by the source cytonemes to the recipient cytonemes in Drosophila wing disc and vertebrate limb buds.
source: In fact, Hh is known to be delivered by the source cytonemes to the recipient cytonemes in Drosophila wing disc and vertebrate limb buds (Chen et al., 2017; González-Méndez et al., 2017; Sanders et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim cites previous work (Chen et al., 2017; González-Méndez et al., 2017; Sanders et al., 2013) showing source cytoneme-mediated delivery of Hh.

claim: The imaging conditions used in this study could not detect Bnl-containing source cytonemes.
source: However, the imaging conditions used in this study could not detect Bnl-containing source cytonemes.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a technical limitation of the study.

claim: Future live imaging analyses are required to elucidate the mechanisms of cytoneme pathfinding.
source: Future live imaging analyses are required to elucidate the mechanisms of cytoneme pathfinding.
evidence: This is a statement about future research directions.

claim: ASP epithelial cells extend a graded number of cytonemes that reach out and contact the disc bnl source to receive the signal.
source: We uncovered that ASP epithelial cells extend a graded number of cytonemes that reach out and contact the disc bnl source to receive the signal (Figure 5A–D'').
evidence: Figure 5A-D'' shows quantitative analysis of cytoneme numbers and contacts from different ASP regions.

claim: Recipient cells close to the source have many long polarized cytonemes, but their numbers gradually reduced as the distance from the source increases.
source: Recipient cells close to the source have many long polarized cytonemes, but their numbers gradually reduced as the distance from the source increases.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the quantitative analysis in Figure 5A-D''.

source: One of the target genes, pntP1, is induced by high Bnl levels in the distal region of the ASP and positively regulates the formation of cytonemes and Btl synthesis (Figure 6B,E).

claim: The target gene cut, which is induced by gradually lower levels of Bnl in the ASP stalk region away from the source, negatively controls cytoneme formation and Btl synthesis.
source: On the other hand, surprisingly, the target gene cut, which is induced by gradually lower levels of Bnl in the ASP stalk region away from the source, negatively controls cytoneme formation (Figure 6C,E; 7A,A'; 8A') and Btl synthesis (Pitsouli and Perrimon, 2013).
evidence: Figure 6C,E shows cut expression in low Bnl region. Figure 7A,A' shows cut negatively regulates cytonemes. Citation to Pitsouli and Perrimon, 2013 supports Btl suppression.

source: Moreover, the transcription factors Cut and PntP1 feedback-inhibit each other's expression to maintain their zones of expression in response to Bnl levels (Figure 6M–P).
evidence: Figure 6M-P shows reciprocal inhibition between Cut and PntP1 in clonal analyses.

claim: The consequence is a regulatory loop that controls the generation and reinforcement of different numbers of cytonemes and levels of Bnl signaling, making the contours of the Bnl gradient robust, precisely tissue-specific, and self-sustaining.
source: The consequence is a regulatory loop that controls the generation and reinforcement of different numbers of cytonemes and levels of Bnl signaling, making the contours of the Bnl gradient robust, precisely tissue-specific, and self-sustaining.
evidence: This is a conclusion integrating all findings on feedback regulation (Figures 6-7) into a proposed mechanism.

claim: One current morphogen model proposes that the signal gradients are generated and scaled to the size of the recipient tissue by the ratio of two diffusible molecules, a morphogen and a contractor/expander, which emanate from opposite poles of the tissue and elicit non-autonomous global feedback to control each other's distribution.
source: One current morphogen model proposes that the signal gradients are generated and scaled to the size of the recipient tissue by the ratio of two diffusible molecules, a morphogen and a contractor/expander, which emanate from opposite poles of the tissue and elicit non-autonomous global feedback to control each other's distribution (Barkai and Shilo, 2009; Ben-Zvi et al., 2011; Restrepo and Basler, 2011; Shilo and Barkai, 2017).
evidence: This claim cites previous work (Barkai and Shilo, 2009; Ben-Zvi et al., 2011; Restrepo and Basler, 2011; Shilo and Barkai, 2017) describing the expander-contractor model for gradient scaling.

claim: Although Cut and PntP1 are intracellular transcription factors that function cell autonomously, their counteracting feedback activities, regulating where and when signal-specific cytonemes are made as a function of the levels of signal received, can self-generate gradients adopting any recipient-specific shape.
source: Although Cut and PntP1 are intracellular transcription factors that function cell autonomously, their counteracting feedback activities, regulating where and when signal-specific cytonemes are made as a function of the levels of signal received, can self-generate gradients adopting any recipient-specific shape (Figures 1F; 8A').
evidence: This conclusion integrates findings on cell-autonomous effects of Cut and PntP1 (Figure 6M-P, 7) with observations of dynamic gradient shapes (Figure 1F). Figure 8A' shows the proposed model.

claim: This mechanism implies an interesting systemic feedback where the gradient shape is a result of the growth and patterning of the recipient tissue, which it controls.
source: This mechanism implies an interesting systemic feedback where the gradient shape is a result of the growth and patterning of the recipient tissue, which it controls.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the implications of the proposed feedback mechanism.

claim: This mechanism also implies that to initiate such a self-sustaining gradient, initial physical contact of a part of the recipient epithelium with the signal source is required.
source: However, this mechanism also implies that to initiate such a self-sustaining gradient, initial physical contact of a part of the recipient epithelium with the signal source is required.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the contact-dependent nature of the mechanism.

claim: Each tracheal cell is capable of inducing either PntP1 or Cut/Yan expression irrespective of its position within the recipient epithelium.
source: In fact, each tracheal cell is capable of inducing either PntP1 or Cut/Yan expression irrespective of its position within the recipient epithelium (Figure 8A).
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from clonal analyses showing that cells can induce these genes when exposed to appropriate Bnl levels regardless of position (Figures 6-7). Figure 8A shows model.

claim: An ectopic new bnl source near a pre-existing tracheal branch can initiate a local gradient of cytoneme contacts leading to polarized signal and signaling gradient formation as well as neo-branch organization.
source: Thus, an ectopic new bnl source near a pre-existing tracheal branch can initiate a local gradient of cytoneme contacts leading to polarized signal and signaling gradient formation as well as neo-branch organization (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is a prediction based on the proposed mechanism. Figure 8B shows model of this scenario.

claim: Spatiotemporal expression of Bnl surrounding the embryonic tracheal placode is known to induce new branches.
source: In agreement with this view, spatiotemporal expression of Bnl surrounding the embryonic tracheal placode is known to induce new branches (Sutherland et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim cites previous work (Sutherland et al., 1996) showing Bnl induces tracheal branching.

claim: If the Bnl response genes are not the same or are not regulated in the same manner at all sites and at all times, different patterns of cytoneme formation can be generated leading to changes in spatial patterns of signal distribution and tissue morphology.
source: Moreover, if the Bnl response genes are not the same or are not regulated in the same manner at all sites and at all times, different patterns of cytoneme formation can be generated leading to changes in spatial patterns of signal distribution and tissue morphology.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about how variations in gene regulation could lead to morphological diversity.

claim: Given the commonality of fundamental signaling events mediated by conserved signaling proteins, feedback regulation of cytoneme-mediated transport may offer an explanation for why signal gradients are so precise, yet adaptable and for how diverse tissue morphologies can result from just one signal transduction pathway.
